title: Hazi Mohd. Yaseen v. P.V.V.N.L. & Another
coram: Amitava Lala & Ashok Srivastava, JJ. (delivered by Amitava Lala, J.)
docket: Civil Misc. Writ Petition No. 27196 of 2011
disposition: Writ petition disposed of (final assessment quashed; remitted for fresh order after personal hearing, on a 50% deposit)
headnote: The 'reasonable opportunity of hearing' required by Section 126(3) of the Electricity Act, 2003 (read with the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005) before a final assessment of electricity theft includes a personal hearing — because an essential service has been disconnected and a theft charge carries penal consequences. An ex parte final assessment, passed without personal hearing, is quashed and remitted for a fresh reasoned order after a personal hearing, on a precondition that the consumer deposit 50% of the claim (mirroring Section 127(2)). While natural justice is not a straitjacket and personal hearing is not required in every case, where the statute contemplates a reasonable opportunity of hearing in the consumer/theft context, personal hearing is essential.

holding_units.topic: Personal hearing is part of 'reasonable opportunity' before a final theft assessment
holding_units.question: Does the 'reasonable opportunity of hearing' under Section 126(3) require a personal hearing before a final assessment of theft, or is taking note of written objections enough?
holding_units.holding: It requires a personal hearing. Merely taking note of written objections is not compliance; because supply (an essential service) has been disconnected and the theft charge carries penal consequences, a personal hearing is essential before a final assessment. The ex parte final assessment is quashed and remitted for a fresh reasoned order after personal hearing, conditioned on the consumer depositing 50% of the claim (25% cash + 25% security).
holding_units.limiting_facts: After two rounds over the provisional assessment, the Executive Engineer passed an ex parte final assessment (2.2.2011) for 407 days without a personal hearing, on an MRI report not supplied to the consumer.

holding_units.topic: Assessment period — entire period of unauthorised use, or 12 months if unascertainable
holding_units.holding: Section 126(5) has two parts: assessment for the entire period during which unauthorised use took place, or, if that period cannot be ascertained, a period limited to twelve months preceding inspection. Whether the period (here 407 days) was properly ascertained is a factual question for the assessing/appellate authority.

principle_tags.application: In the consumer/electricity-theft context, the statutory 'reasonable opportunity of hearing' (s.126(3)) includes a personal hearing before a final assessment; taking note of written objections alone is insufficient.

lead_authorities.name: Transmission Corpn. of A.P. Ltd. v. Sri Rama Krishna Rice Mill
Khem Chand v. Union of India

not_decided.point: Merits of the theft assessment and the meter-seal-tampering inference
not_decided.note: The Court did not decide the merits (or whether tampered cubicle seals per Clause 8.1(b)(i) ipso facto establish theft), leaving them to the fresh assessment/appeal; it declined to go into merits given the alternative remedy.

authorities.name: Transmission Corpn. of A.P. Ltd. v. Sri Rama Krishna Rice Mill
authorities.proposition: In an electricity assessment dispute, merely taking note of the objections filed is not compliance with the relevant rules; natural justice is not a straitjacket formula and varies with the circumstances.
authorities.how_treated: Relied on / discussed for the content of the opportunity of hearing in the consumer-electricity context.

authorities.name: Khem Chand v. Union of India
authorities.proposition: A 'reasonable opportunity' of showing cause includes an opportunity of a personal hearing (in the service-inquiry context).
authorities.how_treated: Discussed and distinguished as a service matter, but its principle supported requiring a personal hearing here.

authorities.name: F.N. Roy v. Collector of Customs, Calcutta
authorities.proposition: There is no rule of natural justice that at every stage a person is entitled to a personal hearing.
authorities.how_treated: Referred (respondent's line) but held not to displace the personal-hearing requirement here.

authorities.name: Union of India v. Jyoti Prakash Mitter
authorities.proposition: Article 217(3) does not guarantee a right of personal hearing; a mere denial of an oral representation does not, without more, vitiate proceedings.
authorities.how_treated: Referred (respondent's line); distinguished as not a consumer-electricity context.

authorities.name: Carborundum Universal Ltd. v. CBDT
authorities.proposition: Where a statutory provision does not exclude natural justice, an opportunity of being heard is to be assumed, especially in quasi-judicial proceedings.

authorities.name: Aligarh Muslim University v. Mansoor Ali Khan
authorities.proposition: Following S.L. Kapoor v. Jagmohan, where on admitted/indisputable facts only one conclusion is possible, breach of natural justice need not vitiate the order (a narrow exception).
authorities.how_treated: Referred (respondent's line); the exception held inapplicable.

authorities.name: Abdus Salam @ A. Salam v. Election Commission of India
authorities.proposition: There is nothing rigid about natural justice; the duty to hear does not always mean affording a personal hearing.

authorities.name: Whirlpool Corporation v. Registrar of Trade Marks, Mumbai
authorities.proposition: The availability of an alternative remedy is no bar to a writ petition where there is a breach of natural justice or an excess of jurisdiction.
authorities.how_treated: Referred (petitioner's line on maintainability despite the s.127 appeal).

authorities.name: Bihar State Electricity Board v. Parmeshwar Kumar Agarwala
authorities.proposition: The Supply Code / conditions of supply have statutory flavour and are to be strictly followed by the parties.
authorities.how_treated: Referred for the statutory character of the Supply Code.
